title: IQP Inspections for Access-Controlled Doors: The Compliance Check Most NZ Building Owners Overlook
description: Every access-controlled door in a New Zealand building with a compliance schedule carries a legal obligation under the Building Act — an annual inspection by an Independently Qualified Person, or IQP. The door must be inspected, tested, and reported to the local council each year, confirming it is performing to its specified standard. In practice, most building owners either do not know this applies to them, or they leave it until a compliance failure surfaces during a council audit. Red Wolf holds IQP qualifications and carries out these inspections as part of a broader access control service. We check that each door is latching, locking, and releasing correctly under all conditions — including alarm activation and power failure. If it is not performing to standard, we fix it and issue the required documentation. With the end of the calendar year approaching, now is a practical time to check whether your compliance schedule is current. If you are not sure whether your doors need an inspection, we can tell you in a short conversation what is required and what it will cost.

title: A New Study Found That Less Than Half of Organisations Are Confident in Their Active Assailant Response — Here Is What NZ Businesses Should Do About It
description: ASIS International and Everbridge released research this week showing that less than half of respondents are highly or mostly confident their staff know what to do in an active assailant incident. Four factors were linked to higher confidence: a comprehensive written plan, regular drills, communications technology, and a functioning behavioural threat assessment and management team. The gap between having a security system and having a prepared organisation is exactly what this finding describes. A camera at the front door and a monitored alarm panel do not tell your staff what to do when something happens. Physical security has two components — the technology layer and the human layer. Most businesses invest in the first and largely ignore the second. The organisations with the highest confidence in their readiness have both: documented procedures, tested regularly, supported by the right technology, and owned by someone with the authority to act. If your business has never run a scenario exercise or reviewed its emergency response documentation, that gap is worth closing before you need it.

title: 91% of Customer-Facing Workers Faced Aggression: What NZ Retailers Should Do
description:
The NZSA has signed the ShopCare Retail Pledge, which formally recognises occupational violence and aggression as a critical risk in retail. The pledge follows the ShopCare National Customer Aggression Survey, which found that 91% of customer-facing workers experienced customer aggression in the past year.

For New Zealand retailers, that figure should change how physical security is scoped. Training and de-escalation come first, but the building has to support staff when a situation escalates. That means duress alarms that are actually monitored and tested. It means CCTV positioned to capture faces at entry and point of sale, not just ceiling-wide coverage. Staff-only areas need access control so a team member can step back behind a locked door. Sightlines matter too: counters and layouts should let staff see trouble coming. In Auckland and Wellington stores, we often see duress buttons that were installed years ago and never tested, or that are mounted where staff can't reach them under pressure.

If you manage retail sites and want an outside view of how your layout and systems protect staff, send us a message to book a review.

title: Who Carries the Risk When Your Security Install Goes Wrong?
description:
When a secured door fails to lock, or an alarm doesn't report, the first question is often about who is accountable. Procurement teams that ask this before signing a contract are in a far better position than those who ask after an incident.

A typical brief we receive from Wellington and Auckland property managers covers more than equipment. They need a provider whose work will stand up to their insurer, their auditors and their tenants. Our approach starts with the paperwork that makes liability clear: documented designs and as-built records. We complete commissioning tests with sign-off, keep maintenance logs and set clear service responsibilities. We work to the professional standards expected of NZSA members, so clients have an industry benchmark to hold us against. The outcome is a system with a defensible record behind it. If something goes wrong, there's evidence of what was installed, how it was tested and when it was last serviced. Without that record, the risk usually falls back on the building owner.

If you're reviewing security contracts or tender requirements, send us a message and we'll walk through what to ask for.

title: ASIS's Revised Workplace Violence Standard: Is Your Building Design Part of It?
description:
ASIS International has released its revised Workplace Violence Prevention and Intervention Standard. It is an ANSI-approved framework for evaluating your current programme, building a plan with clear roles, and sustaining it through continuous improvement.

Most workplace violence programmes we see in New Zealand rely on policy and training, and both are essential. But a plan is only as good as what the building lets people do in the moment. Can a receptionist lock the front entry without leaving the desk? Does a duress alarm go somewhere that will respond? Can staff move to a secure area, and does the intercom let them screen visitors before opening the door? Our position at Red Wolf is that physical controls should be reviewed in the same exercise as the policy, not as a separate project months later. In Wellington and Auckland workplaces, the gap is usually not knowing what to do. It's that the building doesn't support doing it.

Where does your organisation sit: policy first, building first, or genuinely joined up? Drop a comment below.
